seo.title: Yellow Leaves on Plants: 9 Causes and Fixes (2026)
seo.description: Yellow plant leaves, read by pattern: wet mix, dry spells, dim light, hunger, mites, age, cold or a move. A free tool ranks the likely cause. Checked 2026.
seo.h1: Why are my plant leaves turning yellow? 9 causes and the fix for each

answer: Most yellow leaves on a houseplant trace back to too much water: soggy mix starves the roots of oxygen and the plant sheds its oldest leaves first. Push a finger 2 inches into the mix. Wet means stop watering and look at the roots; dry means check light, feeding, pests and age.
intro: A leaf turns yellow when it loses chlorophyll faster than the plant can replace it, and the plant decides which leaves to give up based on what it is short of. That is why the pattern tells you more than the color. Clemson Cooperative Extension says plainly that yellowing is most often a symptom of overwatering, yet it also lists too little light, too little fertilizer, insects and mites, while a long dry spell yellows the lowest leaves too. Old bottom leaves that fade one at a time on a plant still pushing new growth are usually just aging. Yellow spreading through the whole plant, speckled yellow, or yellow on brand new leaves each point somewhere different. This guide sorts the nine common causes by what you can see and touch in a couple of minutes: the moisture of the mix, the position of the yellow leaves, the light at the window and the undersides of the foliage. Each cause comes with a fix you can start today, and the symptom tool above ranks the likely ones for your plant.

tool.title: Pick your plant and the state of the soil: the tool ranks the causes our plant guides give for yellow leaves.

sections.h2: The nine causes at a glance
paras: Start with the mix, not the leaves. A finger pushed 2 inches down, the depth the University of Illinois Extension recommends for deciding when to water, splits the nine causes into two camps within seconds. Wet mix with yellowing points to water or drainage. Dry mix points to thirst, light, food or pests. The table pairs each cause with the sign that gives it away and the first thing to change.

sections.h2: Soggy mix: why it yellows leaves first
paras: Roots breathe. When every pore in the mix is filled with water, they run out of oxygen, stop taking up water and nutrients, and the plant pulls resources out of its oldest leaves to keep the young ones going. The result is yellowing that looks like hunger or thirst while the pot is heavy and wet. Clemson's advice for whole-plant yellowing is direct: check the drainage, look at the roots, and if most are dark, soft and dead, the plant is better discarded.

Several of the plant guides on this site list exactly this pattern. A monstera yellows when it is watered again before the top quarter to third of the mix has dried, a ZZ plant when its rhizomes sit in mix that never dries out, and a rubber plant when the soil stays wet through its fall and winter rest. To tell a drowning plant from a parched one with confidence, use our overwatering vs underwatering guide; if the roots are already brown and mushy, go straight to the root rot guide.

sections.h2: Thirst, light and an empty pot of nutrients
paras: Dryness yellows leaves too, though from the bottom up and more slowly. Clemson notes that lower foliage turns yellow and dies when a plant is left too dry for an extended time, and that chronic underwatering also brings wilting and curled leaves. The leaves usually feel thin or crisp rather than soft, and the pot is light when you lift it.

Light is the cause people overlook most. Clemson puts the bare minimum at about 100 foot-candles for 12 hours a day just to keep a foliage plant looking the same for a year, and at least 200 foot-candles for 12 hours before fertilizer does any good. Clemson adds that the interior of a well-lit home is often below 100 foot-candles. A plant parked in a corner slowly drops its older leaves because it cannot afford to keep them, and new ones come in smaller and paler.

Hunger shows as yellowing, then browning, of the lower leaves. Clemson attributes it mainly to nitrogen or iron deficiency and says pot-bound plants are especially prone, because a pot full of roots holds little mix to supply them. Regular feeding and periodic repotting into fresh mix prevent it. The Illinois Extension schedule is modest: most houseplants need fertilizer no more than once every 1 to 3 months, between March and September, and very little or none in the short days of winter. Feeding a plant that sits in dim light will not green it up; it only adds salts.

Yellow made of tiny dots is a different problem. Spider mites suck sap from the leaf cells and leave light-colored speckling on the upper surface, an overall faded look, and, if left alone, bronzed or yellowed leaves and a dying plant, according to Clemson. Fine silk webbing appears in heavy infestations. Aphids cause yellow, misshapen leaves and sticky honeydew on new growth, and whiteflies yellow and kill leaves in the same way.

Turn a few leaves over under good light before blaming water or food. A magnifier helps, because mites are barely visible. Move the plant away from the others the moment you find anything. The week-by-week treatment plan lives in our houseplant pests guide.

sections.h2: Old leaves, cold nights and a change of address
paras: Some yellowing is simply the plant renewing itself. NC State Extension notes that it is normal for a rubber plant to let some bottom leaves turn yellow and drop, and pothos vines lose older leaves over time until foliage remains only at the tips. The test is balance: one old leaf going while a new one unfurls is housekeeping, five leaves going at once is a symptom.

Temperature matters more than most people think. The Illinois Extension puts the comfort zone for most foliage plants at 65 to 75 degrees by day, 5 to 10 degrees lower at night, and warns against blasts of hot or cold air from vents and against cold window panes, which can damage foliage. UF/IFAS adds that plants kept below 50 degrees for long periods may suffer permanent damage. Clemson lists chilling as a cause of leaf drop.

A move to a new room, a new home or a shop shelf to your windowsill can trigger yellowing and drop as the plant adjusts to a different light level. Clemson says this kind of leaf drop should last only about three weeks. Resist the urge to repot, feed or move it again during that time.

sections.h2: Getting the most from the diagnosis tool
paras: The tool above does not guess. It reads the symptom, cause and remedy tables written for each plant guide on this site, each one sourced, and counts how many plants link yellow leaves to each cause. If you pick your own plant, its own entries weigh three times as much. Your soil reading then shifts the ranking: wet soil doubles the weight of overwatering, poor drainage and disease, and cuts dry-side causes such as underwatering, dry air and heat to less than a third. Dry soil does the reverse.

Read the result as a shortlist, not a verdict. The top line tells you where to look first; the remedy comes from the guide of a plant that actually has that problem. If the tool shows no cause, no plant guide documents that combination yet, and the table at the top of this page is the better starting point.

faq.q: Will yellow leaves turn green again?
faq.a: Rarely, and it is not worth waiting for. Once a leaf has gone fully yellow the plant is reclaiming what it can from it, and Clemson notes that leaves damaged by oedema, one cause of yellowing in wet winter mix, will not recover. A leaf that is only slightly pale from hunger or low light may regain some color after you correct the problem. Judge your fix by the new leaves: if they come in firm and green, the cause is solved.

faq.q: Should I cut off yellow leaves on my plant?
faq.a: Yes, once you have worked out why they turned. A fully yellow leaf will not feed the plant again, and removing it makes it easier to spot whether new yellowing starts. Pull it gently if it comes away with a light tug, or cut the leaf stalk close to the stem with clean scissors. Do not strip half-yellow leaves from a plant that is already struggling with low light or a recent move, because it still draws some energy from them.

faq.q: Can too much fertilizer make leaves turn yellow?
faq.a: It can. The Illinois Extension warns that too much fertilizer can burn roots, especially when growth slows in dim light, and Clemson lists dropping lower leaves among the signs of salt buildup, along with brown leaf tips and wilting. A white crust on the soil or the pot rim confirms it. Run a large volume of plain water through the pot, empty the saucer, and feed no more than once every 1 to 3 months from March to September.

faq.q: Why are only the bottom leaves of my plant turning yellow?
faq.a: Bottom leaves are the oldest, so the plant gives them up first whatever the stress. One at a time, with healthy new growth on top, is normal aging. Several at once usually means wet mix, a long dry spell, or a lack of nitrogen in a pot full of roots, which Clemson names as the usual cause of yellowing and browning lower leaves. Feel the mix 2 inches down: wet, dry or normal points you to the right fix.

faq.q: Why are my plant's leaves turning yellow after I moved it?
faq.a: A new spot means a new light level, temperature and humidity, and the plant sheds leaves it can no longer support while it adjusts. Clemson says leaf drop from a significant change in environment should last only about three weeks. Keep watering by the soil rather than the calendar, avoid feeding or repotting in that window, and keep the plant away from cold glass and heating vents. If yellowing continues past a month, look for another cause.

faq.q: Are yellow leaves with brown spots a sign of disease?
faq.a: Possibly. Clemson describes fungal leaf spots as small brown spots with yellowish margins, sometimes with rings like a target, and bacterial spots as water-soaked patches with a yellow halo. Both spread with splashed water. Remove and discard the spotted leaves, water the mix rather than the foliage, stop misting, and give the plant more air movement. Plain yellowing with no spots is far more often a watering or light problem than a disease.
